---
title: "Similar scores, sharper component contrasts"
output:
  html_document:
    template: common/report.html
    theme: null
    mathjax: null
    self_contained: false
    pandoc_args: ["--wrap=none"]
params:
  prepared_dir: ""
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE)
x<-readRDS(file.path(params$prepared_dir,'score_profile_contrasts.rds'))
esc<-function(v){v<-gsub('&','&amp;',as.character(v),fixed=TRUE);v<-gsub('<','&lt;',v,fixed=TRUE);gsub('>','&gt;',v,fixed=TRUE)}
emit<-function(...)cat(...,sep='')
num<-function(v,d=1)sprintf(paste0('%.',d,'f'),v)
sc<-function(v)sprintf('%+.3f',v)
pc<-function(v)paste0(num(v),'%')
tbl<-function(headers,rows)paste0('<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>',paste(headers,collapse='</th><th>'),'</th></tr></thead><tbody>',paste(vapply(rows,function(r)paste0('<tr><td>',paste(r,collapse='</td><td>'),'</td></tr>'),character(1)),collapse=''),'</tbody></table></div>')
fig<-function(id)paste0('<figure><img alt="Underlying component percentages for the two areas" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,',jsonlite::base64_enc(readBin(file.path(params$prepared_dir,paste0(id,'_presentation.svg')),'raw',n=file.info(file.path(params$prepared_dir,paste0(id,'_presentation.svg')))$size)),'"></figure>')
```

```{r report, results='asis'}
emit('```{=html}\n<style>
*{box-sizing:border-box}body{margin:0;font:16px/1.65 Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;color:#254653;background:#f2f6f8}header{padding:35px max(24px,5vw);background:#173e50;color:white}header h1{font-size:36px;line-height:1.2;margin:8px 0 15px}header p{max-width:1100px;color:#dcecef}nav{display:flex;gap:18px;flex-wrap:wrap}nav a{color:white}main{max-width:1400px;margin:24px auto;padding:0 24px}section{background:white;border:1px solid #dae6ea;border-radius:8px;padding:26px 30px;margin:24px 0}h2{font-size:26px;color:#173e50;line-height:1.3}h3{color:#226273}.callout{background:#edf7f7;border-left:4px solid #16768a;padding:14px 18px}.note{font-size:13px;color:#58707d}.table-wrap{overflow-x:auto}table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:14px}th{text-align:left;background:#edf3f6;padding:11px}td{padding:11px;border-bottom:1px solid #e0eaee;vertical-align:top}tr:nth-child(even){background:#fafcfd}figure{margin:22px 0}figure img{display:block;width:100%;height:auto}details{margin:15px 0;border:1px solid #dae6ea;border-radius:6px;padding:12px}summary{font-weight:bold;color:#236172;cursor:pointer}@media(max-width:750px){main{padding:0 10px}section{padding:20px 14px}header h1{font-size:29px}table{min-width:660px}}@media print{body{background:white}nav{display:none}section{border:0}figure{break-inside:avoid}}
</style><header><h1>Similar scores can conceal sharply different concerns</h1><p>A four-geography check using the existing area-level scores and component percentages. The strongest examples illustrate why the overall score should be read beside its component profile.</p><nav><a href="#overview">Four-geography search</a><a href="#sindh_sharp_demand">Sindh</a><a href="#cdi_broader_demand">Côte d’Ivoire demand</a><a href="#senegal_broad_demand">Senegal</a><a href="#cdi_concentrated_supply">Supply example</a><a href="#methods">Selection and interpretation</a></nav></header><main>')
emit('<section id="overview"><h2>What the search found</h2><p>Across ',x$audit$demand_profiles,' complete demand profiles, <b>no near-equal-score pair</b> combines an area with at least five above-average components and an area where one component supplies at least 70% of positive component points. There are, however, striking examples of similar scores with different percentage profiles. A separate Senegal example shows the broader-versus-concentrated pattern with less similar totals.</p>')
rows<-lapply(seq_len(nrow(x$overview)),function(i){r<-x$overview[i,];c(esc(r$country_label),paste0(esc(r$area_a),' ',sc(r$score_a),'<br>',esc(r$area_b),' ',sc(r$score_b)),num(r$score_gap,3),paste0(esc(if(r$maximum_gap_component=='confidence')x$labels['confidence']else r$maximum_gap_label),'<br>',pc(r$maximum_gap_pct_a),' versus ',pc(r$maximum_gap_pct_b),' (',num(r$maximum_pp),' pp)'),paste0(r$breadth_a,' versus ',r$breadth_b,' of 6'))})
emit(tbl(c('Geography','Areas / demand scores','Score gap','Largest raw-percentage contrast','Above-average components'),rows),'<p class="note">Within each geography, this table selects the near-equal pair with the largest mean absolute percentage-point difference across all six components, requiring at least 50 valid women per domain. The criterion selects illustrative contrasts, not statistical significance or intervention effectiveness. All percentages are survey-weighted among women in need of family planning.</p></section>')
takeaways<-c(
 sindh_sharp_demand='Kemari and Khairpur have nearly identical demand scores. Kemari has much higher low confidence; Khairpur has higher future-fertility concerns and anticipated stigma. This is a clear example of similar totals masking different mixes of concerns, rather than an all-six-versus-one contrast.',
 cdi_broader_demand='Divo has five of six components above their area reference means. Dabou has three: health beliefs, fertility concerns and a small positive opposition component. Health and fertility concerns are each 100% in Dabou, versus 36.5% and 84.1% in Divo. Dabou is a more concentrated health/fertility profile, not a purely single-component case.',
 senegal_broad_demand='Dagana has all six components above their respective reference means. Bignona has two, but the confidence component is much larger than its other positive component. Low confidence is 86.5% in Bignona versus 38.4% in Dagana; future-fertility concerns are 64.0% versus 89.2%. This is the clearer breadth-versus-concentration example, but the overall scores are not near-equal.',
 cdi_concentrated_supply='Abidjan has five unfavorable supply components. Gagnoa has three, but free provision supplies 81.2% of its positive challenge points. Their supply challenge scores differ by 0.095. Gagnoa has stronger recorded LARC stock but weaker free provision and training. Supply strengths can offset weaknesses in the total, even when the unfavorable components differ.')
for(id in names(x$selected)) {
 q<-x$selected[[id]];a<-q$a;b<-q$b;v<-q$components;side<-as.character(q$case$side)
 emit('<section id="',id,'"><h2>',esc(a$country_label),' · ',if(side=='Demand')'reported concerns'else'facility supply profile','</h2>',fig(id),'<div class="callout">',takeaways[id],'</div>')
 for(p in list(a,b))emit('<p class="note"><b>',esc(p$area),':</b> ',if(side=='Demand')paste0(p$n_need,' women in need')else paste0(p$fp_facilities,' confirmed FP facilities'),'; valid component Ns ',p$min_valid,'–',p$max_valid,'. ',p$unfavorable_components,' of six components unfavorable; largest component is ',num(100*p$largest_positive_share),'% of positive component points.</p>')
 if(id=='senegal_broad_demand')emit('<p class="note"><b>Small-sample qualification:</b> Dagana has 55 women in need and 48–55 valid answers per domain. Its estimates are less precise; this case is shown separately from the ≥50-per-domain near-equal-score search.</p>')
 if(id=='cdi_broader_demand')emit('<p class="note"><b>Dabou response pattern:</b> its 59 women in need come from three survey clusters. PB2A records 22 very-likely and 37 quite-likely responses; every woman selects at least one reversible method in MP4. The two 100% values reproduce the raw responses, but the small clustered sample and unanimous classification warrant caution when presenting this example.</p>')
 ca<-v[v$geo==a$geo,];cb<-v[v$geo==b$geo,];cb<-cb[match(ca$variable,cb$variable),]
 rows<-lapply(seq_len(nrow(ca)),function(j)c(esc(x$labels[ca$variable[j]]),paste0(pc(ca$raw_pct[j]),' (n=',ca$n_valid[j],')'),paste0(pc(cb$raw_pct[j]),' (n=',cb$n_valid[j],')'),num(abs(ca$raw_pct[j]-cb$raw_pct[j]))))
 emit('<details><summary>Original percentages and valid denominators</summary>',tbl(c('Component',esc(a$area),esc(b$area),'Absolute difference (pp)'),rows),if(side=='Supply')'<p class="note">Both the graph and table retain the original heatmap percentages: higher is better for the first five components, while lower stockout burden is better. The graph labels the original readiness scores. Shares averaged within facilities are not percentages of facilities; offering and LARC-stock indicators are facility percentages.</p>'else'', '</details></section>')
}
emit('<section id="methods"><h2>How these examples were selected and checked</h2><p><b>Scope:</b> administrative-area planning profiles from the current Lagos, Senegal and Côte d’Ivoire Rural/Urban reports and the current Sindh district report. Supply pools confirmed FP facilities across residence categories within each area. These are not the residence-specific supply exposures or personal demand scores used in the regression models.</p><p><b>Scores:</b> the six original component z-values are averaged. Demand is higher for greater concerns. The supply figure shows original readiness: <b>negative means below-average readiness</b>. Only the technical concentration diagnostic uses its sign-reversed challenge score; for example, readiness −0.188 corresponds to challenge +0.188. No original classifications were changed. Means and SDs use the source report’s equal-area reference distribution within each geography; scores are not comparable across countries.</p><p><b>Exploratory rules:</b> both challenge scores must be positive (equivalently, both original supply readiness scores must be negative), with an absolute gap ≤0.10 original average-z points for a near-equal comparison. “Broader” counts components above their reference means, including small positive differences. “Concentrated” requires a largest-component share ≥70% of the sum of positive component z-values. This share is not a fraction of the net score, a percentage of nonuse explained, or a causal effect. The 0.10, 50/20 valid-response and 70% rules are transparent illustration screens, not validated clinical or precision thresholds.</p><p><b>Supply search:</b> ',x$audit$strict_near_equal_supply_pairs,' pairs meet both breadth/concentration and score-similarity rules, both in Côte d’Ivoire. Abidjan–Gagnoa is shown above. Sindh has only two districts with at least 20 valid facilities on every supply component, so its near-equal supply contrasts do not pass that display screen; sparse training information particularly limits these examples.</p><p><b>Weighting and verification:</b> demand percentages retain the source survey weighting among women in need, with a valid denominator separately for every domain. Facility measures are unweighted averages among confirmed FP providers with valid information separately by measure. Every component average was reconciled against the saved report scores, and source-input hashes were checked unchanged. No raw microdata, models, scores or working reports were modified. The displays are point estimates: no test establishes that the illustrated area differences are statistically resolved.</p><div class="callout"><b>What the evidence adds:</b> a similar total does not imply the same combination of reported concerns or service gaps. Show the component percentages beside the score to keep that composition visible. These cross-sectional profiles describe where to examine the evidence more closely; they do not identify proven causes or binding constraints.</div></section></main>\n```\n')
```
